chunks: From him, from Ismail ibn Mihran, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

When Tahir, the son of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), passed away, the Messenger of Allah forbade Khadijah from weeping. She said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, but the milk was flowing over him, so I cried.' He said: 'Would you not be pleased that you find him standing at the gate of Paradise? When he sees you, he will take your hand and enter you into Paradise, in its purest place and most fragrant.' She said: 'And is that so?' He said: 'Allah, the Most Honourable and the Most Benevolent, is not one to deprive a servant of the fruit of his heart, so that he remains patient, exercises self-restraint, and praises Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and then punishes him.'

key_terms.الدُّرَيْرَةُ: The flowing of milk (indicating she was nursing or had milk in her breasts)
key_terms.ثَمَرَةَ فُؤَادِهِ: The fruit of his heart (referring to the beloved child)
key_terms.خَدِيجَةَ: Khadijah, the wife of the Prophet
key_terms.طَاهِرُ: Tahir, the son of the Prophet
key_terms.يَحْتَسِبَ: To exercise self-restraint and count it as a reward from God

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of 'thamarat al-fu'ad' in Shia tradition regarding the death of children?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) clarifies that the Prophet’s instruction to Khadijah not to weep was not a prohibition of grief, but a redirection of her mourning into hope, as she had already shed tears for their son Tahir. The Imam emphasizes the theological principle that Allah, in His generosity, does not deprive a servant of the 'fruit of their heart' (thamarat al-fu'ad) by demanding excessive sorrow; rather, He rewards patient endurance with reunion in the purest realms of Paradise. This highlights the Shia understanding of balanced grief, where emotional expression is natural but should not overshadow trust in divine recompense.
